https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/ful.text: The Budapest Times Full tank, half measure: government offers diesel drivers a monthly 5,000-forint consolation prize By December, owners of diesel-powered vehicles with a maximum of 150 horsepower will receive a total of 20,000 forints in compensation — the Prime Minister announced on Friday afternoon on his Facebook page. In a video posted alongside the entry, Péter Magyar said the government had decided to provide direct assistance in a targeted and sustainable manner — without causing supply problems or the budget “collapsing” — to the owners and families of nearly one million diesel vehicles who are most affected by the rise in diesel fuel prices. He added that owners of the affected diesel cars under 150 horsepower would receive 5,000 forints per month for September, October, November, and December, amounting to a total of 20,000 forints by December. With this, the government is compensating Hungarian families for the price difference between the previously protected price and the current market price for the typical once-a-month fill-up. He said it is neither their goal nor their responsibility to contribute to fuelling high-performance, expensive vehicles at the expense of Hungarian taxpayers. Private individuals who were registered owners of a diesel passenger car with a maximum of 150 horsepower on 1 January 2026 will therefore receive a total of 20,000 forints in support by the end of December 2026. The support will be paid out in several instalments, with the first instalment arriving in October. Those affected do not need to submit an application; based on the database used by the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) for vehicle tax assessment, the Hungarian State Treasury will automatically transfer the subsidy to the bank account from which the owner paid the vehicle tax. If no such account is available, the amount will be sent to another bank account number on record with NAV, and for those with no bank account on file, the subsidy will be delivered by post. Only one vehicle per person qualifies for the subsidy. For those who purchased a diesel car after 1 January 2026, a different solution for paying out the subsidy is being developed. He announced that the subsidy will be extended to Hungarian primary producers and sole traders, provided the vehicle is registered in the private individual’s name. For farmers working in the fields, the price of diesel is directly built into the costs of production, and a tractor, combine harvester, or other agricultural machinery cannot simply be set aside because fuel has become more expensive. The work must be done, the harvest must be brought in, and the autumn ploughing and sowing must be completed, the Prime Minister listed. He added that for this reason, agricultural users will be able to reclaim the full amount of excise duty built into the price of diesel by the end of this year, and with this measure the government aims to ensure that the rise in global oil prices feeds as little as possible into the costs of Hungarian agricultural production and, from there, into food prices. The Prime Minister also spoke about how the global market situation has changed radically in recent months, and that due to events at the Strait of Hormuz and the ongoing drone strikes against oil refineries in the Russian-Ukrainian war, not only has the global market price of oil risen above 100 dollars, but a diesel shortage has also developed in Europe as a result of Russian gasoil imports. Drivers are feeling the consequences everywhere, from Europe through Asia to America. Fidesz may claim otherwise, but the truth is that despite the price increase, the average price of diesel in Hungary remains among the lowest: in Poland it costs 50 forints more to fill up, in Austria 100 forints more, and in Serbia 30 forints more than in Hungary; diesel is also more expensive in Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Slovenia, and only in Croatia — which has a coastline — is diesel cheaper, though that is expected to last only until Monday, said Péter Magyar. He added that reintroducing a protected price “is not an option at this point,” as in that case there would be no wholesaler willing to import diesel into Hungary, and within a few days a shortage would develop at Hungarian petrol stations. Furthermore, at current prices, introducing a protected price would cost the Hungarian budget approximately 50–100 billion forints per month, which would ultimately have to be paid by Hungarian taxpayers. As he said, in recent days the government consulted with experts and market players, calculated and analysed the available options, and chose a solution that provides targeted support to drivers and farmers. Whatever lies the Fidesz may tell — having done nothing for years between 2022 and 2026, when fuel prices were even higher than they are now — the Tisza government is doing everything in its power to protect Hungarian people from the consequences of a price increase whose causes lie far beyond Hungary’s borders. Where we can, we help, while also preserving the country’s secure fuel supply and the functioning of the budget. This is the essence of responsible governance, said Péter Magyar.
